{"conclusion":"Claim 4 is false. There exist decisive, impartial and responsive rules. In particular one can define a rule (given below) that is decisive and impartial on every admissible profile and is responsive for both criteria. Such rules need not always award the win to the higher total; any rule that satisfies all three properties must depart from “always choose the higher total” on at least 4 admissible profiles (i.e. on at least 4 ordered profiles out of the 12), and I give a rule that attains that minimum.","confidence":0.88,"reasoning":"Setup and notation
- Score-vectors are the four 2-bit vectors: 00, 01, 10, 11. Call them v0=00, v1=01, v2=10, v3=11. The charter forbids identical vectors, so admissible (ordered) profiles are all ordered pairs (A-vector,B-vector) with A≠B; there are 12 admissible ordered profiles.
- DECISIVE: for every admissible ordered profile exactly one winner is named.
- IMPARTIAL: swapping A and B vectors swaps the winner (equivalently: for each unordered pair {s,t} of distinct vectors the rule fixes one of s or t as winner; that choice is then applied symmetrically to the two orderings (s,t) and (t,s)).
- RESPONSIVE (interpreting the phrase as intended): for each criterion i∈{1,2} there exists an admissible ordered profile such that changing one proposal’s score on criterion i (and only that single 0/1 entry) yields another admissible profile and the identity of the winner (A vs B) changes.

1) A concrete decisive, impartial and responsive rule (explicitly checked on every admissible profile)
Define the winner for each unordered pair {si,sj} (6 unordered pairs) as follows (the winner listed is the vector that wins that match):
- {v0,v1}: v0 wins (00 beats 01)
- {v0,v2}: v2 wins (10 beats 00)
- {v0,v3}: v3 wins (11 beats 00)
- {v1,v2}: v2 wins (10 beats 01)
- {v1,v3}: v1 wins (01 beats 11)
- {v2,v3}: v3 wins (11 beats 10)
Extend to ordered profiles: if the input is (A-vector=vx, B-vector=vy) with vx≠vy, the rule names the winner as above (if the chosen unordered-pair winner equals vx then A wins, otherwise B wins). This is a valid decisive rule (exactly one winner for every admissible profile) and by construction impartial (swapping vx and vy swaps the outcome).

Responsiveness (check existence of a profile for each criterion where changing only that criterion flips the A/B winner):
- Criterion 1: take the admissible ordered profile (A=v1=01, B=v0=00). According to the rule {v1,v0} winner is v0, so B wins. Change only A’s criterion-1 score (0→1) to get A=v3=11, leaving B=v0=00; now {v3,v0} winner is v3 so A wins. So changing criterion 1 of A flips the winner (B→A). Thus criterion 1 is responsive.
- Criterion 2: take (A=v0=00, B=v3=11). {v0,v3} winner is v3, so B wins. Change only A’s criterion-2 score (0→1) to A=v1=01, B still v3; then {v1,v3} winner is v1, so A wins. So changing criterion 2 of A flips the winner. Thus criterion 2 is responsive.
Both examples are admissible (vectors remain distinct). Thus the rule is decisive, impartial and responsive. This directly refutes the methodologist’s Claim 4.

2) Does any rule satisfying all three conditions always award the win to the proposal with the higher total score?
No. The rule above already shows a counterexample: consider {v0=00, v1=01}. Totals: v1 has total 1, v0 has total 0. The rule chooses v0 over v1 (so the lower-total vector wins) in both orderings of that pair. Therefore a decisive, impartial and responsive rule need not always award the win to the higher total.

3) Minimal number of admissible profiles on which a 3‑property rule must depart from “choose the higher total”
- Count conventions: admissible profiles are ordered pairs (A,B) with A≠B (12 profiles). A profile “agrees with higher total” if the winner under the rule is the proposal that has the strictly larger total score in that profile. When totals are equal (both total 1), there is no “higher total” and such profiles are not counted as departures.
- Lower bound argument (sketch): if a rule never disagrees with higher totals, the induced unordered-pair orientation must place v3 (11) above everyone, and both v1 and v2 above v0; the orientation is then transitive (a linear order). Such a transitive total-preserving orientation cannot produce the two kinds of single-coordinate flips required for responsiveness of both criteria (one of the two criteria will fail to have any admissible profile where changing only that criterion flips the winner). Therefore the rule must disagree with higher totals on at least one unordered pair. A single unordered disagreement (two ordered-profile departures) still leaves a transitive ordering and one criterion remains unresponsive; so at least two unordered-pair disagreements are necessary. Two unordered-pair disagreements produce at least 4 ordered-profile departures. One can check that two unordered-pair disagreements suffice to get responsiveness for both criteria.
- Achievability: the concrete rule above has exactly two unordered-pair disagreements with the “higher total” principle: {v0,v1} (00 beats 01 even though 01 has higher total) and {v1,v3} (01 beats 11 even though 11 has higher total). Each such unordered disagreement contributes 2 ordered admissible profiles where the lower-total vector wins, hence 4 ordered-profile departures in total. We checked that rule is decisive, impartial and responsive. So 4 is achievable.
Conclusion on minimality: any decisive, impartial and responsive rule must disagree with the “choose higher total” principle on at least 4 admissible ordered profiles, and the example above attains that minimum.

4) What must the panel give up and what it costs
- The methodologist’s reasoning that “DECISIVE + IMPARTIAL + RESPONSIVE is impossible, so the panel must abandon impartiality” is incorrect: impartiality can be kept. What is forced is a different trade-off: to keep impartiality and responsiveness together while making a decisive choice the panel cannot have a rule that always chooses the higher total; it must accept some profiles where the (strictly) lower-total proposal is chosen. Concretely, any rule with the three properties must disagree with the higher-total principle on at least 4 of the 12 admissible ordered profiles. Thus the cost of preserving decisiveness and impartiality together with responsiveness is that the panel must tolerate some (ineliminable) departures from the simple “higher total wins” principle (at least 4 admissible profiles).","uncertainty":"I interpreted "altering only that criterion's score" to mean changing exactly one of the four binary entries (either A's or B's score on that criterion), holding everything else fixed; this is the interpretation used to check responsiveness. If the user intended a different meaning (for example changing a single criterion score on both proposals simultaneously or some other convention), the construction and the minimal-count argument would need to be rechecked under that reading."}

Define the rule by specifying, for each unordered pair of distinct vectors, which vector wins when compared. Use the following pairwise winners (read x vs y: winner is the listed vector):
- 00 vs 01 -> 01
- 00 vs 10 -> 10
- 00 vs 11 -> 00  (this is the single deliberate deviation from higher-total)
- 01 vs 10 -> 10  (tie of totals; break in favor of 10)
- 01 vs 11 -> 11
- 10 vs 11 -> 11
Given these pairwise outcomes, the rule is: for admissible profile (vA,vB), the proposal whose vector is the winner above is selected.
Verify the three properties:
- Decisive: for every admissible (vA,vB) with vA != vB one of the two vectors is designated winner, so the rule picks exactly one proposal.
- Impartial: the rule depends only on the two vectors; whenever x beats y, y does not beat x, so swapping the two vectors swaps the winner. (Equivalently, for the ordered profiles (x,y) and (y,x) the winners are opposite.)
- Responsive: show one witness profile per criterion.
  * First criterion (first bit): take (A,B) = (10,01). According to the rule 10 beats 01, so A wins. Change A's first bit 1->0 to get (00,01); now 01 beats 00, so B wins. A single change of the first criterion changed the winner.
  * Second criterion (second bit): take (A,B) = (10,00). Initially 10 beats 00, so A wins. Change A's second bit 0->1 to get (11,00); by the rule 00 beats 11, so B wins. A single change of the second criterion changed the winner.
Hence the rule is decisive, impartial and responsive. Therefore claim 4 (that no rule can satisfy all three) is false.

Does any such rule always award the win to the proposal with the higher total score? No. The rule above shows a counterexample: in 00 vs 11 the rule awards the win to 00 (total 0) over 11 (total 2). So a decisive, impartial and responsive rule need not always pick the higher total.

Minimal departure from the higher-total principle
- If a rule followed the higher-total principle on every unequal-total pair, the only remaining freedom would be the tie between 01 and 10 (both total 1). But with that single bit of freedom you cannot make both criteria responsive: responsiveness on the first criterion can be achieved by choosing the tie-break one way, responsiveness on the second criterion requires the opposite tie-break. Thus it is impossible to be decisive, impartial and responsive while agreeing with higher-total on all unequal-total pairs.

Therefore the minimal number of admissible profiles on which a rule satisfying all three conditions must depart from the higher-total principle is 2 (one unordered pair -> both orders). The rule given above achieves exactly that: it agrees with higher-total on all unordered unequal-total pairs except 00 vs 11, where it reverses the expected higher-total winner; thus it departs on exactly the two admissible profiles (A=00,B=11) and (A=11,B=00).

What the panel must give up and what it costs
- The panel need not give up impartiality (names can be ignored) — there exist impartial, decisive, responsive rules.
- To keep impartiality and responsiveness, the panel cannot insist that "always pick the proposal with the higher total" on all admissible profiles. At least one unordered unequal-total pair must be reversed; that costs at least two admissible profiles on which the lower-total proposal is chosen.

Note on interpretation and limitation
- I interpreted "altering only that criterion's score" as changing a single proposal's single-bit score on the named criterion (so the new profile must still be admissible). If you use a different interpretation (for example allowing simultaneous changes to both proposals on that criterion only), the concrete construction and the minimal-count argument may need small adjustments, but the core conclusions (claim 4 false; must depart from higher-total on at least one unordered pair) remain the same under the usual reading.",

Represent unordered pairs of distinct vectors {u,v} and for each such pair fix a preferred vector; for ordered profile (u,v) declare A the winner iff the preferred element of {u,v} is u (this construction ensures impartiality and decisiveness automatically).  - Impartial: by construction preferred({u,v}) is an unordered-pair choice; for (u,v) the winner is A iff preferred({u,v})=u, and for (v,u) the same preferred element makes the winner B. Thus swapping names swaps the winner.
 - Responsive: provide witnessing single-bit changes for each criterion:
    * Criterion 1: start at (A,B) = (01,10). Winner is B because preferred({01,10})=10. Change only A’s first bit 0->1 to get (11,10). Now preferred({11,10})=11, so winner becomes A. Winner changed by altering criterion 1.
    * Criterion 2: start at (A,B) = (00,10). Winner is A because preferred({00,10})=00. Change only A’s second bit 0->1 to get (01,10). Now preferred({01,10})=10, so winner becomes B. Winner changed by altering criterion 2.
